# Sequence files: FASTQ and FASTA {#sec-sequence-files}

Two plain-text formats hold DNA sequence: **FASTQ** (your reads, with a
quality score for every base) and **FASTA** (reference sequences, without
qualities). This chapter opens each one and goes through it line by line.

## FASTQ

### What it looks like

```bash
zcat $DATA/N61311_untrt_R1_001.fastq.gz | head -8     # or: gzip -dc ... | head -8
```

```
@A00123:456:HXXXXDSX2:1:1101:10004:1000 1:N:0:ACGTACGT+TGCATGCA
TTGCAGGTCTTCAGCAGTTCCTTGAACTCGTCCAGGTTGATCTTGGCCTTCAGGTTGTCG
+
FFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFF,FFFFFFFFFFFFFF
@A00123:456:HXXXXDSX2:1:1101:10022:1000 1:N:0:ACGTACGT+TGCATGCA
GCCCAGCAGGAGCTGGAGAAGGCCAAGGAGGAGCTGCAGGCGCAGCTGGAGCAGGCCACA
+
FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
```

(Example reads from a modern instrument. The practice data come from a
public archive, which adds its own prefix: `@SRR1039508.1 HWI-ST177:290:C0TECACXX:1:1101:1225:2130/1`.
After the run accession, it's the same kind of name.) Each read
is exactly **four lines**:

| Line | Starts with | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `@` | The read's name (header) |
| 2 | | The bases: `A`, `C`, `G`, `T`, and `N` when the machine couldn't decide |
| 3 | `+` | A separator (sometimes followed by the name again) |
| 4 | | One quality character per base, so it is exactly as long as line 2 |

### The header, piece by piece

Illumina headers follow a fixed pattern:

```
@A00123:456:HXXXXDSX2:1:1101:10004:1000 1:N:0:ACGTACGT+TGCATGCA
 └──┬─┘ └┬┘ └───┬───┘ ┬ └┬─┘ └─┬─┘ └┬─┘ ┬ ┬ ┬ └──────┬────────┘
 instrument  flow cell lane tile  x    y read filt ctrl  index (i7+i5)
         run number                    1/2  Y/N
```

- Everything **before the space** identifies the cluster. It is the same in
  R1 and R2 for the two reads of a pair. That is how tools check pairing.
- **Read** `1` or `2` says which end this is.
- **Filtered** `N` means the read passed Illumina's quality filter (`Y` reads
  are normally already removed).
- **Index** is the barcode that was used to demultiplex this read.

### Quality scores

Each quality character is a number written as a single character. The
number is a **Phred quality score** Q:

$$
Q = -10 \log_{10}(P_\text{error})
$$

| Q | Chance the base is wrong | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 1 in 10 | 90 % |
| 20 | 1 in 100 | 99 % |
| 30 | 1 in 1,000 | 99.9 % |
| 40 | 1 in 10,000 | 99.99 % |

To save space, Q is stored as the character whose ASCII code is Q + 33
("Phred+33", used by every modern instrument):

| Character | `!` | `+` | `5` | `?` | `:` | `F` | `I` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 25 | 37 | 40 |

NovaSeq and NextSeq 2000 **bin** qualities into just a few values, which is
why their quality lines are mostly `F` with a few `:` and `,` (Q 37, 25, 11).

::: {.callout-note}
You will never decode these by hand. FastQC and Trim Galore do it. But it
explains why a FASTQ quality line looks like random punctuation.
:::

### R1 and R2 are a matched pair of files

For paired-end data you get two files, and **line *n* of one belongs with
line *n* of the other**. If one file is truncated, filtered on its own or
re-sorted, the pairing breaks. A quick check:

```bash
zcat sample_R1_001.fastq.gz | head -1
zcat sample_R2_001.fastq.gz | head -1
# the part before the space must be identical
```

### Useful things to do with FASTQ

```bash
# count reads (lines / 4)
echo $(( $(zcat R1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))

# look at only the sequences of the first 5 reads
zcat R1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | head -5

# read length distribution of the first 10,000 reads (after trimming, lengths vary)
zcat R1_trimmed.fastq.gz | head -40000 | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {print length($0)}' | sort -n | uniq -c

# take the first 100,000 read pairs to make a small test set (keep R1 and R2 in step!)
zcat R1.fastq.gz | head -400000 | gzip > test_R1.fastq.gz
zcat R2.fastq.gz | head -400000 | gzip > test_R2.fastq.gz
```

**seqkit** is a fast all-purpose tool for FASTQ/FASTA (in the `rnaseq-tools` environment):

```bash
seqkit stats *.fastq.gz          # reads, bases, min/avg/max length per file
seqkit grep -p "A00123:456:HXXXXDSX2:1:1101:10004:1000" -r R1.fastq.gz   # find one read
```

## FASTA

### What it looks like

```
>chr1
NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN
...
TAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCC
>chr2
...
```

- A line starting with `>` is a **header**: the name of the sequence that follows.
- The following lines are the sequence, usually wrapped at 60 or 80
  characters per line. A sequence continues until the next `>`.
- No quality line: a reference is assumed correct.
- `N` marks bases that are unknown in the assembly (telomeres, centromeres, gaps).
- **Lowercase** bases (`acgt`), when present, mark repeats (*soft-masking*).
  Aligners treat them like uppercase.

### Genome FASTA vs transcriptome FASTA

| | Genome FASTA | Transcriptome FASTA |
|---|---|---|
| One entry per | chromosome / contig | transcript (every isoform) |
| Size (human) | ~3 Gb | ~400 Mb |
| Introns? | yes | no: exons only, already spliced |
| Used by | HISAT2, STAR | Salmon, kallisto |

A GENCODE transcriptome header packs several IDs together, separated by `|`:

```
>ENST00000456328.2|ENSG00000290825.1|-|-|DDX11L2-202|DDX11L2|1657|lncRNA|
 transcript ID      gene ID              transcript  gene   length biotype
                                         name        name
```

### Genome builds and chromosome names

A **genome build** (also called an assembly) is one version of the reference
sequence. Coordinates from one build are **not valid** in another.

| Species | Builds you'll see | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Human | **GRCh38 = hg38** (current), GRCh37 = hg19 (old) | bagPipes' references are hg38 |
| Mouse | GRCm39 = mm39 (current), GRCm38 = mm10 (old, still common) | |

Two naming styles exist for the same chromosomes: **UCSC** uses `chr1`, `chrM`;
**Ensembl** uses `1`, `MT`. GENCODE files use the UCSC style. Every file you
combine (FASTA, GTF, BED, bigWig) must use the same style, or tools will
find "no overlap" without raising an error.

::: {.callout-note}
## "Primary assembly"

The full human assembly also includes *alternate haplotypes*: extra copies of
some regions with population variants. Reads that fall there look like
multi-mappers. Pipelines usually use the **primary assembly** (chromosomes,
unplaced contigs, no alternates), which is what `gencode.v49.primary_assembly`
means in the bagPipes config.
:::

### Useful things to do with FASTA

```bash
samtools faidx genome.fa                 # build genome.fa.fai (an index)
cut -f1,2 genome.fa.fai | head           # chromosome names and lengths
samtools faidx genome.fa chr7:5527148-5530601   # pull out a region (here: around ACTB)
grep -c ">" transcripts.fa               # how many transcripts
seqkit stats genome.fa
```

The `.fai` index is a small table: name, length, and where in the file each
sequence starts. IGV and many tools need it next to the FASTA.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. A quality character is `5`. What is the chance that base is wrong?
2. Why do the headers of the two reads in a pair match up to the space?
3. You align to a genome whose FASTA says `>1`, and load a BED file that says
   `chr1`. What happens?
4. Why does Salmon use a transcriptome FASTA while HISAT2 uses the genome?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. `5` is Q20, so 1 in 100.
2. They are two reads of the **same cluster** (the same DNA fragment); the
   name identifies the cluster, the part after the space says which read.
3. Nothing overlaps: the tools treat `1` and `chr1` as different chromosomes.
   Usually there's no error message, just empty results.
4. Salmon asks "which transcript did this read come from?" and needs the
   spliced transcript sequences. HISAT2 asks "where in the genome?" and has to
   handle introns itself ([Alignment](alignment.qmd)).
:::
:::
